title: People I Know
full_review:
"People I Know" (Miramax) is a disappointing thriller about a washed-up celebrity publicist (Al Pacino) who finds himself a pawn in a dangerous game involving a murdered starlet -- a crime implicating members of New York's mover and shaker elite. Director Dan Algrant's noirish foray into Gotham's shadowy netherworld of glamour and politics is mired by a hackneyed, disjointed narrative and a lead performance that at times flirts close to hammy.

Eli Wurman (Pacino) is running on fumes. An old-school press agent, his once-impressive stable of celebrity clients has all flown the coop, leaving him hanging out to dry. He has watched the media parade he helped create pass him by through his cadaverous, sleep-deprived eyes, dulled by booze and designer pharmaceuticals. He survives on the graces of his last paying client, Cary Launer (Ryan O'Neal), a world-famous movie star with political aspirations.

At one point Wurman states that he has no soul, yet it is evident early on that he is the only character with any sense of moral conscience -- visually reinforced by the framed photos plastering his walls documenting his proclivity for social activism.

The trouble begins when Launer solicits a "favor" from Wurman, which loosely translated means cleaning up a mess -- more often than not, involving some dame. This particular mess requires posting bail for a pill-popping prima donna, Jilli Hopper (Tea Leoni). The fading flack, loath to bite the hand that feeds him, agrees to help Launer out of the jam, with one stipulation -- in return, Launer must make an appearance at a civil rights benefit Wurman is organizing -- a vestige from his freedom-marching glory days.

The floozy is sprung without a hitch. But afterward she demands they make a stop at a surreal floating opium den to retrieve her "toy" -- a scene straight out of Kubrick's "Eyes Wide Shut." Back at her hotel suite things get ugly. In a deadly turn of events Jilli is murdered, while, unbeknownst to her assassin, a semi-conscious Wurman watches, passed out in her bathroom. The crime is made to look like an overdose.

It doesn't take Sherlock Holmes to figure out Jilli's killer was after her toy -- a Gameboy-like gizmo Wurman had inadvertently slipped into his own pocket. Later, viewers learn that it contains scandalous digital photos that could prove damaging in an upcoming election -- though exactly who they incriminate remains a mystery, unresolved by the film's end.

This peccadillo is excused as the film's "McGuffin" -- a term coined by Alfred Hitchcock to indicate the object sought by the characters which serves as a device to set the action in motion.

Left with only hazy, narcotized recollections of the previous evening and Jilli's enigmatic toy, Wurman unwittingly becomes entangled in a labyrinth of cover-ups and conspiracies orchestrated by unseen powers -- only now he is in their cross hairs.

Ignoring his deteriorating health, Wurman plunges head-on with his benefit, pleading and cajoling celebrities and politicians -- "people I know" -- to show up at the event. They include an incendiary Harlem minister (Bill Nunn) and a civic-minded billionaire (Richard Schiff) with more than a few skeletons in his closet. Wurman begins to unravel, unable to trust anyone -- unsure if the next morning's newspaper will carry his obituary.

Wedged messily into all this is a subplot involving Wurman's widowed sister-in-law (Kim Basinger), a southern belle wheedling him to return to the bucolic simplicity of Dixieland.

Sound a tad confusing? Don't fret; it is.

The mood of the film has a hand-me-down quality, borrowing generously from earlier political thrillers like Alan J. Pakula's "The Parallax View"; a poster of the 1974 suspense yarn is featured prominently in Wurman's office. And while the mystique of cabals and conspiracies usually proves entertaining, the suspicion and political paranoia which fuel much of the overstuffed plot won't produce the same resonance that Pakula's film did in the post-Watergate climate -- those days, too, have passed Wurman by.

Many of the film's obligatory twists, including extraneous characters making veiled threats, seem to purposely obscure the cliche-laden narrative rather than piloting it to a coherent denouement.

Pacino's gravelly performance, which entails staggering through most of the film looking like an unmade bed and sounding like Rhett Butler on valium, feels like a retread from his more recent oeuvre. As a consummate professional, however, the understated gravitas he brings to the role makes many of the movie's defects less glaring.

Due to minimal violence, recurring drug abuse, rough language and vulgarities, as well as brief sexual images and fleeting nudity, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III - adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
